title: Indian IT Firms Hold Cash Collection Steady as Clients Slow New Deals
excerpt: Average days sales outstanding improved marginally to about 75 days, even as cautious client spending lengthens the road from deal approval to revenue.
body:
• Average days sales outstanding (DSO) across leading Indian IT services firms improved marginally from 76 days to about 75 days, according to UnearthInsight data reported by The Hindu BusinessLine on November 16.
  • TCS held its DSO at 74 days, Infosys edged up from 63 to 64 days, HCLTech improved from 86 to 84 days, and Persistent improved from 86 to 74 days.
  • Analysts say longer deal approvals and cautious discretionary spending have not translated into delayed payments for work already delivered.
  • For investors, the pressure point the analysts identify is not collections but conversion: how long new deals take to win approval, start and turn into revenue.

Longer deal approval cycles and cautious technology spending have yet to significantly affect payment cycles for Indian IT services companies, with average days sales outstanding across leading players remaining broadly stable, according to The Hindu BusinessLine. DSO measures how many days, on average, a company takes to collect payment after billing a client, so a stable DSO means reported revenue is turning into cash at roughly the same speed as before.

According to UnearthInsight, TCS has maintained its DSO at 74 days, while Infosys has seen a marginal increase from 63 to 64 days. HCLTech has improved from 86 to 84 days, while Tech Mahindra and Coforge have increased by four and two days respectively. Persistent has recorded an improvement from 86 to 74 days. Overall, the average across these companies improved marginally from 76 days to approximately 75 days.

What the analysts say

Gaurav Vasu, chief executive and founder of UnearthInsight, said there is not enough evidence to suggest a broad-based deterioration in client payment behaviour.

"While discretionary technology spending remains cautious and decision-making cycles have become longer, this does not necessarily translate into delayed payments for work already delivered."

— Gaurav Vasu, CEO and Founder, UnearthInsight

The bigger challenge for IT services firms currently, Vasu said, is the time taken for new deals to receive approvals, commence execution and convert into revenue, rather than slower payments from existing clients. Biswajit Maity, a senior principal analyst at Gartner, said providers with recurring services, regular billing and diversified client portfolios generally have more predictable cash collection, while DSO is more volatile for companies exposed to large milestone-based projects, complex contracts and concentrated customer bases. Gartner has no evidence, he said, that companies are broadly accepting longer payment cycles or weaker payment terms to drive growth.

Why the numbers differ by company

DSO differences are driven by a combination of geography mix, industry vertical mix, contract structures and the efficiency of individual companies' collection teams, the BusinessLine report says. HCLTech has a relatively higher exposure to engineering, research and development and manufacturing clients, where payment cycles typically range between 80 and 85 days. Hi-tech clients tend to pay faster, even when contracts carry 90-day payment terms, while clients in telecom and retail often use the full contractual payment window of 85 to 90 days. "A higher DSO does not necessarily indicate weaker collection discipline, but also reflects the underlying client and business mix of each company," Vasu said.

The cautious client behind the numbers

The collection data lands in a quarter when clients are plainly taking longer to say yes. Mint reported on November 16 that India's mid-sized IT firms, including Persistent, have called out slower deal decisions amid geopolitical uncertainty, and that Infosys chief financial officer Jayesh Sanghrajka told the company's analyst call on October 23 that client spending remains cautious, with the West Asia conflict, inflation and tariffs constraining discretionary spend and extending decision cycles. Providers are responding with greater commercial flexibility to win or retain strategic work in AI, cloud, cybersecurity and modernisation, including phased delivery, longer ramp-up periods, milestone billing and flexible pricing, according to Gartner's Maity.

What to watch

Vasu's conclusion is that companies may offer some commercial flexibility to secure strategic accounts or large deals, but cash flow discipline remains important, because accepting substantially longer payment cycles would add to working capital requirements at a time when pricing pressure is already squeezing margins. The next test is conversion, not collection: whether the deals now sitting in longer approval cycles start, and start billing, in the quarters ahead.
